mainText:
If you only remember one thing: the midterms showed that A I infrastructure is now a ballot box issue.

Number one. Voters turn on data centers. From your Rundown. Data center opponents won thirty eight of thirty nine fully counted local ballot measures. In the N B C exit poll, seventy six percent of voters said they would oppose a data center in their own community. And fifty seven percent expect A I to do more harm than good. Goldman Sachs reportedly sees forty five percent of planned U S data center capacity at risk of temporary freezes. Voters also handed Congress to Democrats, promising tougher oversight of Silicon Valley. Why it matters: public opinion, not just regulation, is now a real limit on how fast A I gets built.

Number two. Grok Bot starts making phone calls. From your Rundown. Paid users can now have the bot sit on hold, book appointments, and negotiate bills on U S phone numbers. The user is legally the caller of record, and is responsible for every call. The bot says it is a virtual assistant. Early examples include a cable bill negotiation and a pizza order. Why it matters: when an A I agent acts for you, the legal responsibility lands on you, and that is a big open question for A I policy.

Number three. Apple opens up Siri. From your Rundown, plus web reports. Apple is reportedly letting third party A I chatbots plug into Siri in i O S twenty seven. This comes from reports, not an official launch. Why it matters: it could shift power in the A I assistant race away from single vendor lock in.

Number four. Chips and China. Recent web reporting says the U S Commerce Department has tightened A I chip license rules for companies headquartered in China, even when they operate abroad. I could not confirm the exact date, so treat this as an ongoing story. Why it matters: export controls are now about who owns the data center, not only where it sits.

Number five. Also in your Reads. The New Yorker Daily looks at a new definition of Alzheimer's disease, and whether new drugs really help. John Cutler's Beautiful Mess covers game design and consulting as product work. And James Clear's newsletter is on finding the right career.

Number six. The good news close. The data center backlash shows that communities have a real voice in how A I gets built, and that is a healthy check. One note: Readwise was unavailable this run, so no saved articles are included.

And the thread today: A I is moving out of the lab and into the voting booth, the phone line, and the supply chain. That's your briefing. Have a great day.
